warmup.q: A primary streams to one asynchronous standby that runs about 50 ms behind. The primary's disk dies at 10:42:07, and ops promotes the standby a minute later. What happened to the payments whose clients saw them commit at 10:42:06.98?
options: They are on the new primary: PostgreSQL acknowledges a commit only once a standby has it
They are probably lost: an asynchronous primary acknowledges a commit once its own WAL is on disk, and the last 50 ms of WAL never reached the standby
They are lost only if the standby was running read-only queries at the time
The promotion fetches them from the dead primary's WAL automatically
warmup.why: This is lesson 1's asynchronous failover on a real system. PostgreSQL replicates asynchronously by default: COMMIT returns when the primary's WAL is flushed, and the walsender ships it a moment later. Commits inside that moment exist only on the dead disk, so the promoted standby never sees them, although their clients were told they committed. Only a synchronous standby (synchronous_commit on or remote_apply with synchronous_standby_names set) closes the gap. Promotion only replays WAL the standby already received; it cannot reach a dead server.

sections.h: A standby is a second server that replays the primary's WAL
sections.html:
This lesson runs the track's first three lessons on one real system. Lesson 1 built single-leader replication: one ordered log, followers at a position in it, a choice of when the leader says OK, a new follower from a snapshot plus a position, and a failover that can lose writes. Lesson 2 showed that PostgreSQL's log is its physical WAL. Lesson 3 showed what lag does to reads. Here is how PostgreSQL 18 does each of them, plus the one thing replication can't give you: a backup.

PostgreSQL builds its followers, which it calls standbys, from machinery it already has. Every change is appended to the write-ahead log first, and after a crash the server replays that log from the last checkpoint onto its data files (the Storage track's lesson on write-ahead logging and crash recovery). Now take a copy of the data directory and never let its recovery end: feed it the primary's WAL as the primary writes it, and it replays each record onto the same 8 KB pages. That copy is a standby. It is physical, byte for byte: the same pages, the same row positions, the same major version.

Three pieces build one, and this lesson's Compose file, env/postgres-ha.yml, uses all three:

  • pg_basebackup -h primary -U replicator -D $PGDATA -X stream -S standby1 -R copies the running primary's data directory over a replication connection, plus the WAL written while it copies (-X stream). The role needs the REPLICATION attribute and a pg_hba.conf line with the keyword replication.
  • -R writes an empty standby.signal, which makes the server start in standby mode and stay in recovery, and adds primary_conninfo (host, port, user, password) to postgresql.auto.conf.
  • -S standby1 streams through a replication slot, a record on the primary of the oldest WAL position that standby still needs (restart_lsn).

Started, the standby runs a walreceiver that connects to the primary, and the primary forks a walsender for it. The walsender sends WAL as soon as it is written; the walreceiver writes it to the standby's own pg_wal and flushes it; the startup process replays it. Lesson 1's positions are LSNs (log sequence numbers) here: byte offsets into the WAL, printed like 0/508F830, and pg_wal_lsn_diff subtracts two of them.

The slot matters when a standby stops. Without one, each checkpoint lets the primary remove old WAL whether a standby has it or not, and a standby that was down too long gets requested WAL segment ... has already been removed: it must be rebuilt from a new base backup. With a slot, the primary keeps all WAL from restart_lsn on. That is also the danger: a slot whose standby is gone for good holds WAL forever, until pg_wal fills the disk and the primary stops. Drop slots you no longer use, and set max_slot_wal_keep_size (default -1, no limit) or PostgreSQL 18's idle_replication_slot_timeout (default 0, off), so the primary gives up on a slot before the disk gives up on the primary. This is lesson 1's choice between keeping the log for a follower and rebuilding the follower. With the standby stopped and the timeout at 10 seconds, the next checkpoint chose the rebuild:

 slot_name | active | wal_status | invalidation_reason
-----------+--------+------------+---------------------
 standby1  | f      | lost       | idle_timeout

-- the standby's log when it came back
FATAL:  could not start WAL streaming: ERROR:  can no longer access replication slot "standby1"
DETAIL:  This replication slot has been invalidated due to "idle_timeout".

On the primary, pg_stat_replication has a row per standby with three positions, and the figure shows where each is measured: write_lsn, WAL the standby has handed to its operating system; flush_lsn, WAL on its disk; replay_lsn, what queries on it can see. write_lag, flush_lag and replay_lag give the same distances in time.

try.title: Watch a standby follow, then stop it replaying
steps: Start the two servers from the labs folder: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml up -d --wait. The first start takes about 20 seconds: initdb on the primary, then pg_basebackup for the standby. Then ask the primary about its standby and its slot, and look at the processes on both: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary ps -u postgres -o pid,cmd and the same with standby. docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec standby bash -c 'cat $PGDATA/postgresql.auto.conf' shows what -R wrote.

Open psql on each in its own terminal: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course and docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec standby psql -U sfz -d course. Run the session below, switching terminals at each comment.
Before the count on the standby, predict it: replay is paused, but is the WAL there?

code.title: psql on the primary and on the standby
code.html: -- primary \x on SELECT application_name, client_addr, state, sent_lsn, write_lsn, flush_lsn, replay_lsn, write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag, sync_state FROM pg_stat_replication; SELECT slot_name, slot_type, active, restart_lsn, wal_status FROM pg_replication_slots; \x off INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (1, 500, 'customer_request', now()) RETURNING refund_id; -- standby SELECT refund_id, amount_minor FROM refunds ORDER BY refund_id DESC LIMIT 1; INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (1, 1, 'duplicate', now()); SELECT pg_wal_replay_pause(); SELECT pg_get_wal_replay_pause_state(); -- primary INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) SELECT 2, 100, 'customer_request', now() FROM generate_series(1, 1000); SELECT application_name, sent_lsn, write_lsn, flush_lsn, replay_lsn, pg_wal_lsn_diff(sent_lsn, replay_lsn) AS replay_behind_bytes, write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication; -- standby SELECT count(*) FROM refunds; SELECT pg_wal_replay_resume(); SELECT count(*) FROM refunds;

try.expect:
The primary has one standby, streaming and caught up, and an active slot (your LSNs differ):

application_name | standby1
client_addr      | 172.21.0.3
state            | streaming
sent_lsn         | 0/508DB48
write_lsn        | 0/508DB48
flush_lsn        | 0/508DB48
replay_lsn       | 0/508DB48
write_lag        |
flush_lag        |
replay_lag       |
sync_state       | async

slot_name   | standby1
slot_type   | physical
active      | t
restart_lsn | 0/508DB48
wal_status  | reserved

The lag columns show the last lag measured, a fraction of a millisecond, or nothing once the standby has caught up and nothing new arrives. In ps, the primary has postgres: walsender replicator 172.21.0.3(60024) streaming 0/508F830 and an archiver; the standby has postgres: standby1: startup recovering 000000010000000000000005 and postgres: standby1: walreceiver streaming 0/508F830. The new refund (id 7) is on the standby at once, and the standby refuses to write: ERROR: cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction. With replay paused (paused) and 1,000 rows inserted:

application_name    | standby1
sent_lsn            | 0/5111380
write_lsn           | 0/5111380
flush_lsn           | 0/5111380
replay_lsn          | 0/50E13E0
replay_behind_bytes | 196512
write_lag           | 00:00:00.002436
flush_lag           | 00:00:00.007326
replay_lag          | 00:00:02.702068

The standby received and flushed every byte (write and flush lag of 2 and 7 ms) and replayed none of the 192 KB: its count is still 7. replay_lag only changes when the standby reports a new replay position, so while replay is paused, trust replay_behind_bytes. After pg_wal_replay_resume() it is 1007, at once, because the WAL was already on its disk.

sections.h: Synchronous commit: what a COMMIT waits for, and what each choice loses
sections.html:
Lesson 1's dial between asynchronous and synchronous is two settings in PostgreSQL. By default replication is asynchronous: the primary answers COMMIT as soon as the commit's WAL is on its own disk, and the walsender ships it a moment later; write_lag was 2 ms in the first Try it. If the primary dies inside that moment, the standby never gets those commits. After a failover they are gone, and their clients were told they had committed. For a payment the card network already approved, that is money the ledger no longer knows about.

Synchronous replication closes the gap. Name the standby in synchronous_standby_names on the primary, and every COMMIT waits until that standby confirms. synchronous_commit (default on) chooses what it must confirm:

synchronous_commit COMMIT returns once lost if the primary dies and you fail over
off the WAL is in the primary's memory; the WAL writer flushes it within 3 × wal_writer_delay, 600 ms up to 600 ms of commits, even with no failover
local the WAL is on the primary's disk whatever the standby had not received
remote_write the standby has handed it to its operating system nothing, unless the standby's OS crashes too
on the standby has flushed it to its disk nothing
remote_apply the standby has replayed it nothing, and a read on the standby sees it at once

With synchronous_standby_names empty, every level from remote_write up behaves like local. The list takes one name, FIRST 1 (s1, s2) for the first connected standby in the list, or ANY 1 (s1, s2) for whichever confirms first.

The price is a round trip to the standby, and its fsync, on every commit. In this lesson's containers a commit took about 1.6 ms with local and 6 to 7 ms waiting for the standby. Between two zones of a cloud region, add about a millisecond; between regions, about 70.

The trap is a synchronous standby that is down. Unlike MySQL's semi-sync in lesson 1, PostgreSQL never falls back to asynchronous on its own; the primary holds every COMMIT for as long as that lasts: in this section's Try it, an INSERT hung for 28 seconds until it was cancelled. statement_timeout does not end the wait, because its clock stops before the commit. A cancel does, with a warning that says exactly what happened: The transaction has already committed locally, but might not have been replicated to the standby. The row is on the primary, visible to everyone. Synchronous replication delays the answer; it never undoes a commit.

So run it with two standbys and ANY 1 (s1, s2), so that one can be down, or let the HA tool fall back to asynchronous when the last standby fails, which reopens the gap. And choose per transaction: SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = local for a page-view log, on for the payment.

While the standby is down, its slot holds WAL on the primary: in the Try it, one million new rows left 92 MB in pg_wal that no checkpoint could remove.

try.title: Stop the standby: async fills the disk, sync stops the commits
steps: Start the servers if they are not running (docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml up -d --wait, from the labs folder) and open psql on the primary (docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course). In another terminal, stop the standby: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml stop standby.

Run the first block: the slot query, a million rows, a checkpoint, the slot query again. Then make standby1 synchronous and insert a refund. When it hangs, wait about 20 seconds and press Ctrl+C. Did the refund commit?
Start the standby again (docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml start standby) and run the last block. The last three statements put the primary back as it was.

code.title: psql on the primary
code.html: SELECT slot_name, active, wal_status, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained FROM pg_replication_slots; SELECT count(*) AS files, pg_size_pretty(sum(size)) AS pg_wal FROM pg_ls_waldir(); CREATE TABLE wal_filler AS SELECT g AS id, md5(g::text) AS pad FROM generate_series(1, 1000000) AS g; CHECKPOINT; SELECT slot_name, active, wal_status, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained FROM pg_replication_slots; SELECT count(*) AS files, pg_size_pretty(sum(size)) AS pg_wal FROM pg_ls_waldir(); ALTER SYSTEM SET synchronous_standby_names = 'standby1'; SELECT pg_reload_conf(); \timing on SET statement_timeout = '5s'; INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (3, 250, 'duplicate', now()); -- hangs: Ctrl+C after about 20 seconds SELECT count(*) FROM refunds WHERE payment_id = 3 AND amount_minor = 250; BEGIN; SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = local; INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (3, 260, 'duplicate', now()); COMMIT; -- after: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml start standby SELECT application_name, state, sync_state FROM pg_stat_replication; INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (3, 280, 'duplicate', now()); ALTER SYSTEM RESET synchronous_standby_names; SELECT pg_reload_conf(); DROP TABLE wal_filler;

try.expect:
With the standby stopped, the slot is inactive and holds nothing yet; after a million rows and a checkpoint it holds 92 MB, and pg_wal has grown from 80 MB to 160 MB:

 slot_name | active | wal_status | retained
-----------+--------+------------+----------
 standby1  | f      | reserved   | 0 bytes
 files | pg_wal
-------+--------
     6 | 80 MB
SELECT 1000000
CHECKPOINT
 standby1  | f      | reserved   | 92 MB
    11 | 160 MB

The synchronous INSERT waits, past the 5-second statement_timeout, until you cancel it; psql prints Cancel request sent, then:

WARNING:  canceling wait for synchronous replication due to user request
DETAIL:  The transaction has already committed locally, but might not have been replicated to the standby.
INSERT 0 1
Time: 28645.510 ms (00:28.646)
 count
-------
     1

The refund committed: the count finds it. The SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = local transaction commits in 7.8 ms with the standby still down. Right after the standby starts it shows catchup | potential and the next commit waits for it to catch up (1.1 s in one run); a few seconds later it shows streaming | sync, and a commit takes about 6.8 ms. Your times differ; the waiting does not.

sections.h: Reads on a standby, and the queries replay has to cancel
sections.html:
A standby is not idle. With hot_standby = on, the default, it accepts read-only queries while it replays, so reports, exports and dashboard reads can run there and leave the primary to the writes. Anything that writes fails with ERROR: cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction. Every read sees the data as of the last replayed record, so lesson 3's anomalies all apply: a read just after a write on the primary can miss it. Lesson 3's fixes are PostgreSQL functions here: compare pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() with the LSN of the session's last commit, or commit with remote_apply so the standby has replayed it before COMMIT returns.

Replay and reads collide. PostgreSQL keeps the old versions of updated and deleted rows while some transaction might still read them, and VACUUM on the primary removes them once no transaction on the primary needs them (the Transactions track's lesson on MVCC explains why the old versions exist). The primary knows nothing of the standby's queries, and a report on the standby that started at 10:00 may still need a version the primary removed at 10:05. When the standby reaches that cleanup record in the WAL, it has two choices: stop replaying until the report ends, or cancel the report. It waits up to max_standby_streaming_delay, 30 s by default and 5 s in this lesson's Compose file, then cancels:

ERROR:  canceling statement due to conflict with recovery
DETAIL:  User query might have needed to see row versions that must be removed.

DDL conflicts the same way: ALTER TABLE or DROP TABLE on the primary takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, and replaying it cancels standby queries on that table. pg_stat_database_conflicts on the standby counts each kind.

Each fix moves the cost somewhere else. hot_standby_feedback = on makes the standby report its oldest snapshot to the primary, and VACUUM keeps those versions: no more cancels, but a 3-hour report now keeps 3 hours of dead rows in the primary's tables. A large max_standby_streaming_delay lets reports finish while the standby falls behind, so a failover first has to replay the backlog, and every remote_apply commit waits for it. For long analytics, use a standby of its own with a long delay, where lag hurts nobody, and keep the failover standby close to the primary.

try.title: A report on the standby loses to VACUUM on the primary
steps: Start the servers if they are not running (docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml up -d --wait, from the labs folder). Open psql on each in its own terminal: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course and docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec standby psql -U sfz -d course.
On the primary, give the report something to read: INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) SELECT 2, 100, 'customer_request', now() FROM generate_series(1, 1000);.
On the standby, start the report: a REPEATABLE READ transaction keeps one snapshot. While it sleeps, delete and vacuum on the primary. Predict when the standby's sleep ends.

code.title: psql on the standby and on the primary
code.html: -- standby \timing on BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; SELECT count(*) FROM refunds; SELECT pg_sleep(15); -- primary, while the standby sleeps DELETE FROM refunds WHERE payment_id = 2; VACUUM refunds; -- standby, after the error SELECT count(*) FROM refunds; ROLLBACK; SELECT datname, confl_snapshot, confl_lock FROM pg_stat_database_conflicts WHERE datname = 'course';

try.expect:
The count depends on what earlier Try-its inserted (1,013 rows here). The 15-second sleep ends early, about 5 seconds after the VACUUM:

SELECT pg_sleep(15);
ERROR:  canceling statement due to conflict with recovery
DETAIL:  User query might have needed to see row versions that must be removed.
Time: 7045.483 ms (00:07.045)
SELECT count(*) FROM refunds;
ERROR:  current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block
ROLLBACK
 datname | confl_snapshot | confl_lock
---------+----------------+------------
 course  |              1 |          0

The primary's VACUUM removed the deleted versions, the standby's snapshot still needed them, and after max_standby_streaming_delay (5 s here) replay won. The whole transaction is aborted, not only the statement, and the conflict is counted as a snapshot conflict.

sections.h: Failover: promote the standby, and keep the old primary out
sections.html:
Lesson 1's failover has three steps: notice, choose, redirect. PostgreSQL does none of them. It replicates, and it does not decide when to fail over: nothing in it notices that the primary is gone. A person or a tool notices and runs SELECT pg_promote() on the standby (or pg_ctl promote). The standby replays the WAL it already has, ends recovery, starts a new timeline and accepts writes; in one run of the Try it, that took 214 ms. The timeline number is part of every WAL file name (00000002... after the first promotion), so WAL written after the split never mixes with the old primary's.

What a promotion loses follows from the last section. With asynchronous replication it loses every commit the primary acknowledged and never sent. The Try it widens that gap on purpose by stopping the standby first, and refund 3333 is lost: its client saw INSERT 0 1, and the new primary has never heard of it.

Then the old primary comes back: a host that rebooted, a network partition that healed. It still believes it is the primary, on timeline 1, and accepts writes. Two primaries are split brain, and the Try it shows how fast that corrupts meaning: both servers hand out refund id 40, one for 4444 and one for 5555. Nothing merges them later. So a failover needs fencing: before the standby takes over, make sure the old primary cannot accept writes, by stopping it, cutting it off the network or pulling it out of the load balancer. The PostgreSQL documentation calls it STONITH, shoot the other node in the head. To bring the old primary back as a standby, pg_rewind rewinds its data directory to the point where the timelines split, throwing away its unsent commits (it needs page checksums or wal_log_hints, and checksums are on by default since PostgreSQL 18); otherwise, rebuild it with pg_basebackup.

Clients have to find the new primary. pgJDBC takes several hosts and connects to whichever one accepts writes:

HikariConfig().apply {
    jdbcUrl = "jdbc:postgresql://db-a:5432,db-b:5432/payments?targetServerType=primary"
    connectionTimeout = 2_000      // during a failover, borrows fail fast and the caller retries
}

Doing this by hand at 3 a.m. is slow and easy to get wrong, so most teams automate it with Patroni. A Patroni agent runs next to each PostgreSQL and keeps a leader key in a consensus store: etcd, Consul, ZooKeeper or Kubernetes. The key has a time to live, 30 seconds by default, and the primary's agent renews it every loop_wait, 10 seconds. If the primary dies, or loses touch with the store, the key expires and the standbys' agents race for it. The store agrees by majority (Raft, in etcd's case, which the Consistency and consensus track builds), so exactly one agent wins, and it promotes its PostgreSQL. A primary whose agent cannot renew the key is demoted to read-only: that is the fence. maximum_lag_on_failover keeps standbys that are too far behind out of the race (lesson 1's "choose the most up-to-date follower"), and synchronous_mode makes Patroni promote only a synchronous standby.

Managed services, such as Amazon RDS and Aurora, Google Cloud SQL and Azure Database for PostgreSQL, run the standby, the failover, the fencing and the backups for you; you pick the options and pay for them. The client side stays yours: short connection timeouts, retries for the transactions a failover cuts off, and knowing whether your option is synchronous.

frames.say: Both servers are up. The service writes to the primary; refund 7 (1111) commits there, and the walsender streams the WAL to the standby, which replays it a few milliseconds later. Replication is asynchronous, the default.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 340" role="img" aria-label="The standby is behind and the primary acknowledges a commit it alone has"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><rect class="box" x="260" y="16" width="180" height="48" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="350.0" y="45.0" text-anchor="middle">payments service</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="100" width="300" height="176" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="170" y="124" text-anchor="middle">primary</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="170" y="144" text-anchor="middle">timeline 1</text><text class="t-s" x="44" y="174" text-anchor="start">refund 7: 1111</text><text class="t-s t-a" x="44" y="196" text-anchor="start">refund 8: 3333</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="170" y="262" text-anchor="middle">told the client: INSERT 0 1</text><rect class="box-dim" x="380" y="100" width="300" height="176" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="530" y="124" text-anchor="middle">standby</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="530" y="144" text-anchor="middle">stopped (lag, cut off)</text><text class="t-s" x="404" y="174" text-anchor="start">refund 7: 1111</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="530" y="262" text-anchor="middle">has WAL up to 0/5003FB0</text><path class="ln-a" d="M300 64L170 98" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln-d" x1="320" y1="160" x2="377" y2="160"/><text class="t-s t-a" x="20" y="322" text-anchor="start">Asynchronous: refund 8 is acknowledged though no standby has it.</text></svg>
frames.say: The standby falls behind: here it is stopped, in real life it is lagging or cut off for a moment. Refund 8 (3333) commits on the primary, and because nothing waits for a standby, the client hears INSERT 0 1.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 340" role="img" aria-label="The primary dies with a commit only on its own disk"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><rect class="box" x="260" y="16" width="180" height="48" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="350.0" y="45.0" text-anchor="middle">payments service</text><rect class="box-bad" x="20" y="100" width="300" height="176" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="170" y="124" text-anchor="middle">primary</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="170" y="144" text-anchor="middle">killed</text><text class="t-s" x="44" y="174" text-anchor="start">refund 7: 1111</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="44" y="196" text-anchor="start">refund 8: 3333</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="170" y="262" text-anchor="middle">refund 8 is only on this disk</text><rect class="box-dim" x="380" y="100" width="300" height="176" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="530" y="124" text-anchor="middle">standby</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="530" y="144" text-anchor="middle">stopped</text><text class="t-s" x="404" y="174" text-anchor="start">refund 7: 1111</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="530" y="262" text-anchor="middle">has WAL up to 0/5003FB0</text><path class="ln-bad" d="M300 64L170 98" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><text class="t-s t-a" x="20" y="322" text-anchor="start">The primary dies. Nothing in PostgreSQL notices or decides what to do.</text></svg>
frames.say: The primary dies (docker compose kill, like a power cut). Refund 8 exists only on its disk. PostgreSQL has no component that notices this or picks a successor: a person or a tool must.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 340" role="img" aria-label="The standby is promoted and the commit is lost"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><rect class="box" x="260" y="16" width="180" height="48" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="350.0" y="45.0" text-anchor="middle">payments service</text><rect class="box-dim" x="20" y="100" width="300" height="176" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="170" y="124" text-anchor="middle">old primary</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="170" y="144" text-anchor="middle">down</text><text class="t-s" x="44" y="174" text-anchor="start">refund 7: 1111</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="44" y="196" text-anchor="start">refund 8: 3333</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="170" y="262" text-anchor="middle">not reachable</text><rect class="box-a" x="380" y="100" width="300" height="176" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="530" y="124" text-anchor="middle">new primary</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="530" y="144" text-anchor="middle">pg_promote(): timeline 2</text><text class="t-s" x="404" y="174" text-anchor="start">refund 7: 1111</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="404" y="196" text-anchor="start">refund 8: lost</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="530" y="262" text-anchor="middle">redo done at 0/5003FB0</text><text class="t-s t-a" x="20" y="322" text-anchor="start">Promoted in 214 ms. Refund 8 never left the old disk: it is lost.</text></svg>
frames.say: Someone runs SELECT pg_promote() on the standby. It replays the WAL it has (redo done at 0/5003FB0), picks a new timeline (selected new timeline ID: 2) and accepts writes, 214 ms later. Refund 8 was acknowledged and is not here: that is what asynchronous replication can lose.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 340" role="img" aria-label="The service writes to the new primary"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><rect class="box" x="260" y="16" width="180" height="48" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="350.0" y="45.0" text-anchor="middle">payments service</text><rect class="box-dim" x="20" y="100" width="300" height="176" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="170" y="124" text-anchor="middle">old primary</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="170" y="144" text-anchor="middle">down</text><text class="t-s" x="44" y="174" text-anchor="start">refund 7: 1111</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="44" y="196" text-anchor="start">refund 8: 3333</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="170" y="262" text-anchor="middle">not reachable</text><rect class="box-a" x="380" y="100" width="300" height="176" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="530" y="124" text-anchor="middle">new primary</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="530" y="144" text-anchor="middle">timeline 2</text><text class="t-s" x="404" y="174" text-anchor="start">refund 7: 1111</text><text class="t-s t-a" x="404" y="196" text-anchor="start">refund 40: 4444</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="530" y="262" text-anchor="middle">accepts writes</text><path class="ln-a" d="M400 64L530 98" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><text class="t-s t-a" x="20" y="322" text-anchor="start">The service moves to the new primary. The next refund gets id 40.</text></svg>
frames.say: The service reconnects to the new primary and keeps working. The next refund gets id 40: a sequence logs values ahead in the WAL, and the standby continued from the last value it had seen logged.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 340" role="img" aria-label="The old primary returns and two primaries accept writes"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><rect class="box" x="260" y="16" width="180" height="48" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="350.0" y="45.0" text-anchor="middle">payments service</text><rect class="box-bad" x="20" y="100" width="300" height="176" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="170" y="124" text-anchor="middle">old primary</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="170" y="144" text-anchor="middle">back, still timeline 1</text><text class="t-s" x="44" y="174" text-anchor="start">refund 7: 1111</text><text class="t-s" x="44" y="196" text-anchor="start">refund 8: 3333</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="44" y="218" text-anchor="start">refund 40: 5555</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="170" y="262" text-anchor="middle">accepts writes too</text><rect class="box" x="380" y="100" width="300" height="176" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="530" y="124" text-anchor="middle">new primary</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="530" y="144" text-anchor="middle">timeline 2</text><text class="t-s" x="404" y="174" text-anchor="start">refund 7: 1111</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="404" y="196" text-anchor="start">refund 40: 4444</text><text class="t-s" x="530" y="262" text-anchor="middle">accepts writes</text><path class="ln-bad" d="M300 64L170 98" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><path class="ln" d="M400 64L530 98" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><text class="t-s t-a" x="20" y="322" text-anchor="start">Split brain: two primaries, and refund 40 means two different refunds.</text></svg>
frames.say: The old primary's host comes back, and PostgreSQL starts as what it was: a primary on timeline 1, with refund 8. A pod that still has its address writes refund 5555, and it gets id 40 too. Two servers accept writes and disagree about what refund 40 is. That is split brain, and nothing merges it later.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 340" role="img" aria-label="The old primary is fenced, rewound and made a standby"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><rect class="box" x="260" y="16" width="180" height="48" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="350.0" y="45.0" text-anchor="middle">payments service</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="100" width="300" height="176" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="170" y="124" text-anchor="middle">old primary</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="170" y="144" text-anchor="middle">fenced, pg_rewind, standby</text><text class="t-s" x="44" y="174" text-anchor="start">refund 7: 1111</text><text class="t-s t-a" x="44" y="196" text-anchor="start">refund 40: 4444</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="170" y="262" text-anchor="middle">follows timeline 2</text><rect class="box-a" x="380" y="100" width="300" height="176" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="530" y="124" text-anchor="middle">new primary</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="530" y="144" text-anchor="middle">timeline 2</text><text class="t-s" x="404" y="174" text-anchor="start">refund 7: 1111</text><text class="t-s" x="404" y="196" text-anchor="start">refund 40: 4444</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="530" y="262" text-anchor="middle">the only one that writes</text><path class="ln-a" d="M400 64L530 98" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln-a" x1="380" y1="160" x2="323" y2="160" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><text class="t-s t-a" x="351" y="150" text-anchor="middle">WAL</text><text class="t-s t-a" x="20" y="322" text-anchor="start">Fence first. Rewound, the old primary follows the new one; its refund 8 is gone.</text></svg>
frames.say: The fix is to fence before you promote: stop the old primary or cut it off, so it cannot take writes. To bring it back, pg_rewind rewinds its data directory to where the timelines split, which throws away refund 8, and it restarts as a standby of the new primary. Patroni does the fencing by demoting any primary that cannot renew its leader key.

try.title: Promote the standby, lose a refund, then meet two primaries
steps: Start from fresh servers: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml down -v, then docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml up -d --wait, from the labs folder.
Run the commands below in order. Before the promotion, predict which refunds the new primary will have.
When you are done, docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml down -v deletes both servers.

code.title: in the labs folder
code.html: # 1. a refund that reaches the standby docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course -c "INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (4, 1111, 'customer_request', now()) RETURNING refund_id" docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec standby psql -U sfz -d course -c "SELECT refund_id, amount_minor FROM refunds WHERE refund_id > 6" # 2. the standby falls behind (stopped), a refund commits, the primary dies docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml stop standby docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course -c "INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (4, 3333, 'customer_request', now()) RETURNING refund_id" docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml kill primary # 3. start the standby alone and promote it docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml up -d --wait --no-deps standby docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec standby psql -U sfz -d course -c "SELECT pg_promote()" \ -c "SELECT refund_id, amount_minor FROM refunds WHERE refund_id > 6" -c "INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (4, 4444, 'customer_request', now()) RETURNING refund_id" docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml logs standby | grep -E "promote|redo done|timeline ID: 2" # 4. the old primary comes back docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml start primary docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course -c "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery()" -c "INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (4, 5555, 'customer_request', now()) RETURNING refund_id" docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course -c "SELECT refund_id, amount_minor FROM refunds WHERE refund_id > 6" docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec standby psql -U sfz -d course -c "SELECT refund_id, amount_minor FROM refunds WHERE refund_id > 6"

try.expect:
Refund 7 (1111) reaches the standby. Refund 8 (3333) is acknowledged by the primary with the standby stopped. After the kill and the promotion, the new primary has refund 7 only, and gives the next refund id 40:

 pg_promote
------------
 t
 refund_id | amount_minor
-----------+--------------
         7 |         1111
 refund_id
-----------
        40
-- the log, prefixes trimmed
LOG:  received promote request
LOG:  redo done at 0/5003FB0 system usage: CPU: user: 0.00 s, system: 0.00 s, elapsed: 3.03 s
LOG:  selected new timeline ID: 2

The old primary starts as a primary (pg_is_in_recovery is f) and also gives id 40 to the next refund. The two servers now disagree:

-- old primary
 refund_id | amount_minor
-----------+--------------
         7 |         1111
         8 |         3333
        40 |         5555
-- new primary
 refund_id | amount_minor
-----------+--------------
         7 |         1111
        40 |         4444

Refund 8 is the commit asynchronous replication lost. Refund 40 is split brain: two primaries, one id, two different refunds. Ids jump from 8 to 40 because a sequence logs 32 values ahead in the WAL, and both servers continued from the same logged value.

sections.h: Backups: a dump, or a base backup plus the WAL archive
sections.html:
A standby is not a backup. Run DELETE FROM merchant_fee_schedules without its WHERE clause, and the standby deletes the same rows a few milliseconds later. A backup is a copy from the past, and there are two kinds.

A logical backup is SQL. pg_dump -Fc -d course -f course.dump reads one database through one consistent snapshot, without blocking writers, and writes the definitions and rows of its tables: 33 KB in 0.2 s for the course database. pg_restore loads it into the same or a later major version, the whole database or one table, in parallel with -j. Roles belong to the cluster, so they need pg_dumpall --globals-only as well. A dump is only as fresh as its last run, and restoring it means inserting every row and rebuilding every index: fine for gigabytes, hours for terabytes.

A physical backup is the data directory plus the WAL. pg_basebackup takes the base backup, exactly as it built the standby. Continuous archiving keeps the WAL: with archive_mode = on, the archiver process runs archive_command for each finished 16 MB segment, here test ! -f /archive/%f && cp %p /archive/%f, and the primary keeps a segment until the command returns 0. On a quiet server a segment can take hours to fill, so set archive_timeout to bound how old the archive gets.

To restore, copy the base backup into an empty data directory, set restore_command to fetch segments back from the archive, create recovery.signal, and start. The server replays the archived WAL like a standby that knows when to stop: with recovery_target_time, it stops before the first commit after that time, promotes itself onto a new timeline, and opens. That is point-in-time recovery (PITR): last night's base backup, plus the WAL up to the second before the bad DELETE. In the Try it the restored server logged recovery stopping before commit of transaction 865 and had all 8 fee schedules back.

Tools do the bookkeeping cp does not. pgBackRest, Barman and WAL-G compress, encrypt and verify, keep a retention schedule, and restore in parallel, and PostgreSQL 17 added incremental base backups (pg_basebackup --incremental, then pg_combinebackup). A backup you have never restored is a hope: restore one on a schedule into a scratch server, run row counts and a few known queries, and time it. That time is how long you would be down; the age of the newest archived segment is how much you would lose.

Logical replication is lesson 2's row log: CREATE PUBLICATION pay FOR TABLE payments, refunds on the source, CREATE SUBSCRIPTION ... PUBLICATION pay on the target. The target can run another major version, hold only some tables and take writes of its own. It needs wal_level = logical and a replica identity on every table, and it copies no schema changes and no sequence values (as of PostgreSQL 18). Use it to upgrade with minutes of downtime or to feed a reporting database, not as the copy you fail over to.

What PostgreSQL 18 (September 2025) changed for replication and recovery:

Area PostgreSQL 18
Slots idle_replication_slot_timeout invalidates slots idle for too long (the first section)
pg_rewind data checksums are on by default in initdb, which pg_rewind needs
Monitoring pg_stat_io counts WAL I/O, including the walreceiver's writes on a standby
Logical replication generated columns can be published (publish_generated_columns); CREATE SUBSCRIPTION streams large transactions in parallel by default; apply conflicts are logged and counted in pg_stat_subscription_stats
Tools pg_createsubscriber --all turns a physical standby into logical replicas of every database; pg_upgrade --swap and kept planner statistics shorten upgrades

PostgreSQL 19, at release candidate as this is written, adds logical replication of sequences and a WAIT FOR LSN command for lesson 3's read-your-writes wait.

A checklist for the payments cluster:

  • at least one standby, with a slot, max_slot_wal_keep_size or idle_replication_slot_timeout set, and alerts on replay lag and on inactive slots;
  • synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (s1, s2)' over two standbys, or a written decision to accept what asynchronous replication can lose;
  • automatic failover with fencing (Patroni or a managed service), and a planned switchover rehearsed regularly;
  • clients with a multi-host URL or one stable endpoint, short timeouts, and retries made safe by idempotency keys;
  • base backups plus continuous WAL archiving to another site, archive_timeout set, failed archiving alerted;
  • a scheduled restore test, with its duration written down.

try.title: Undo an accidental DELETE with point-in-time recovery
steps: Start from fresh servers: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml down -v, then docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml up -d --wait, from the labs folder. Take a base backup into the archive volume, next to the archived WAL: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec -u postgres primary pg_basebackup -U sfz -D /archive/base -c fast -P.
Open psql on the primary (docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course) and run the session below. Copy the time before_the_mistake prints.

Recover to that time in a third server, restore: TARGET_TIME='2026-11-08 02:30:12.69231+00' docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml --profile pitr up -d --wait restore, with your time. Read its log: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml --profile pitr logs restore.

Check the restored server, then copy the rows back to the primary: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml --profile pitr exec -T restore pg_dump -U sfz -d course --data-only -t merchant_fee_schedules | docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec -T primary psql -U sfz -d course. Finish with docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml --profile pitr down -v.

code.title: psql on the primary, then on the restored server
code.html: -- primary: a refund after the base backup, then the mistake INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (7, 900, 'customer_request', now()) RETURNING refund_id; SELECT count(*) FROM merchant_fee_schedules; SELECT now() AS before_the_mistake; SELECT pg_sleep(1); DELETE FROM merchant_fee_schedules; -- the cleanup script forgot its WHERE SELECT pg_switch_wal(); -- close the segment so the archiver copies it now -- restore: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml --profile pitr exec restore psql -U sfz -d course SELECT count(*) FROM merchant_fee_schedules; SELECT refund_id, amount_minor FROM refunds ORDER BY refund_id DESC LIMIT 2; SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();

try.expect:
On the primary: refund 7, 8 fee schedules, the time, DELETE 8, and the LSN where the segment closed (yours differ):

 refund_id
-----------
         7
 count
-------
     8
      before_the_mistake
------------------------------
 2026-11-08 02:30:12.69231+00
DELETE 8
 pg_switch_wal
---------------
 0/804E350

The restore server's log, trimmed and without prefixes (the cp: cannot stat lines are restore_command being asked for files that do not exist, which is normal):

restore: copying the base backup, recovering to 2026-11-08 02:30:12.69231+00
LOG:  restored log file "000000010000000000000006" from archive
LOG:  starting point-in-time recovery to 2026-11-08 02:30:12.69231+00
LOG:  restored log file "000000010000000000000007" from archive
LOG:  restored log file "000000010000000000000008" from archive
LOG:  consistent recovery state reached at 0/6000120
LOG:  recovery stopping before commit of transaction 865, time 2026-11-08 02:30:13.697982+00
LOG:  selected new timeline ID: 2
LOG:  archive recovery complete
LOG:  database system is ready to accept connections

Transaction 865 is the DELETE, committed one second after the target. On the restored server the count is 8, refund 7 is there (it came from the WAL, not the backup, which is older), and pg_is_in_recovery is f: it promoted itself. The copy back prints COPY 8, and the primary has its fee schedules again. The base backup took a few seconds; a pg_dump -Fc of the same database is 33 KB and takes 0.2 s, but could only have brought back last night.

refs.title: PostgreSQL 18: Continuous archiving and point-in-time recovery

analogy: Think of the primary as the head clerk who writes every payment into the ledger, and the standby as a second clerk in another building who copies each line as the head clerk reads it to him over the phone. Asynchronous: the head clerk tells the customer "done" as soon as the line is in his own book. Synchronous: he waits until the second clerk says "written". If the head office burns, the second clerk's book becomes the ledger, minus whatever was said into the phone after the line went dead. If the head clerk turns up next day and keeps writing in his old book, there are two ledgers. And a backup is last night's photocopy of the book plus a recording of every phone call, which you can play back up to the minute before someone crossed out a page. The analogy breaks at what is copied: the clerk copies meaning, while a standby copies bytes of pages, so it can never skip one bad entry, and two books that drifted apart can never be merged.
world: At work, Oracle Data Guard plays the standby's part, and the compare below maps its protection modes to synchronous_commit. For a payments service on PostgreSQL, decide per kind of write: an authorization the card network approved should not live on one disk, so give the cluster two standbys and ANY 1 (s1, s2), while a page-view log can use SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = local. Point Quarkus or Hikari at a multi-host URL with targetServerType=primary, keep connectionTimeout short, and make every write retryable: after a failover a client may not know whether its COMMIT landed, which is what the idempotency key and ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO NOTHING from the SQL track's lesson on upserts are for. Temporal retries activities on its own, so the activity that writes the payment must be idempotent for the same reason. A Kafka consumer that commits offsets after the database write may see the same message again after a failover and must not apply it twice. Reports and exports belong on a standby of their own, not on the one you fail over to, and any read that follows a write needs lesson 3's LSN check.
mistake: Forgetting a replication slot. A team retires a reporting standby by shutting its VM down and nothing else. Its slot stays on the primary, inactive, with a restart_lsn that never moves again, so no checkpoint may remove WAL after it. pg_wal grows by the day's WAL every day, 50 GB in a busy week, and one night the disk is full, the primary cannot write WAL, and it stops. It happens because the slot lives on the primary and the standby's owners never look there. Drop the slot when you retire the standby (SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('reports1')), alert when pg_replication_slots.active is false for more than a few minutes, and set max_slot_wal_keep_size, or on PostgreSQL 18 idle_replication_slot_timeout, so that a forgotten slot is invalidated (wal_status lost) before the disk fills.

compare.title: Shipping the log to a standby: Oracle Data Guard and PostgreSQL

a.label: Oracle Data Guard
a.title: Oracle AI Database 26ai
a.html:
transport: redo shipped to the standby
  LOG_ARCHIVE_DEST_2='SERVICE=stby SYNC AFFIRM'
standby: managed recovery applies the redo
  open read-only while applying: Active Data
  Guard, a separately licensed option

protection modes
  MAXIMUM PERFORMANCE   async (the default)
  MAXIMUM AVAILABILITY  sync, but carries on as
                        async if no standby answers
  MAXIMUM PROTECTION    sync; the primary shuts down
                        rather than commit unprotected

failover: the Data Guard broker; Fast-Start
  Failover, where an observer process decides
backups: RMAN, with block-level incrementals

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: PostgreSQL 18
b.html:
transport: WAL streamed by a walsender to the
  standby's walreceiver (primary_conninfo, a slot)
standby: the startup process replays the WAL
  open read-only while replaying: hot_standby,
  on by default

synchronous_standby_names and synchronous_commit
  empty                 async (the default)
  'ANY 1 (s1, s2)', on  sync; commits wait while no
                        listed standby answers, with
                        no automatic fallback
  (Patroni can fall back to async; with
   synchronous_mode_strict it never does)

failover: none built in; pg_promote(), or Patroni
  with etcd, Consul or ZooKeeper as the referee
backups: pg_basebackup and archive_command,
  pgBackRest or Barman; incrementals since 17

compare.note: The mechanism is the same: ship the redo log and replay it on a copy. Three things differ in practice. Oracle's maximum availability mode drops to asynchronous by itself when no standby answers; PostgreSQL's synchronous replication keeps every commit waiting until someone changes synchronous_standby_names, which is safer for data and worse for uptime unless you run two standbys or let Patroni decide. Reading from the standby is built into PostgreSQL; Oracle sells it as Active Data Guard. And Oracle ships its own failover referee (the Fast-Start Failover observer), while PostgreSQL leaves that to an outside tool and a consensus store.

worked.title: A manual failover runbook for the payments cluster

steps.say: Before anything else, make sure the old primary cannot take writes, even if it is only unreachable from where you stand. Check from two places, then fence it: stop it if you can reach the host, or take it out of the load balancer and block its port.
steps.code: # 1. is it really gone? ask from two networks pg_isready -h db-a -p 5432 # from the app subnet pg_isready -h db-a -p 5432 # from the admin host # fence: stop it, or cut it off ssh db-a 'sudo systemctl stop postgresql' || ssh lb 'disable-backend db-a'

steps.say: Pick the standby with the most WAL on its disk. Compare the receive positions, not the replay positions: promotion replays everything received first.
steps.code: -- 2. on each standby SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn() AS received, pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() AS replayed, pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS last_commit_replayed; -- db-b: 2/1A0031C8 db-c: 2/19FF2000 -> promote db-b

steps.say: Promote it and check that it now writes. pg_promote waits up to 60 seconds by default and returns false if promotion did not finish.
steps.code: -- 3. on db-b SELECT pg_promote(wait => true, wait_seconds => 60); -- t SELECT pg_is_in_recovery(); -- f: it is a primary SELECT pg_create_physical_replication_slot('db_c', true); SELECT pg_create_physical_replication_slot('db_a', true);

steps.say: Point the other standby at the new primary. primary_conninfo takes effect on reload (context sighup), and with recovery_target_timeline = 'latest', the default, the standby follows timeline 2.
steps.code: -- 4. on db-c ALTER SYSTEM SET primary_conninfo = 'host=db-b port=5432 user=replicator application_name=db_c'; ALTER SYSTEM SET primary_slot_name = 'db_c'; SELECT pg_reload_conf();

steps.say: Bring the old primary back as a standby, never as a primary. pg_rewind rewinds it to where the timelines split; whatever it committed after that is discarded, so look at it first if you need to know what was lost (the deeper section shows how).
steps.code: # 5. on db-a, PostgreSQL stopped pg_rewind --target-pgdata=/var/lib/postgresql/18/main \ --source-server='host=db-b port=5432 user=postgres dbname=postgres' --progress touch /var/lib/postgresql/18/main/standby.signal # primary_conninfo = 'host=db-b ...' and primary_slot_name = 'db_a' in postgresql.auto.conf, then start it

lab.title: A model of streaming replication: replay, commit waits, slots, failover and PITR
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder; they need no Docker. All 27 fail. Streaming.kt gives you a Primary that commits WAL records with LSNs, Standbys cloned from a base backup, and a Cluster whose stream ships records the way a walsender does. Read it first.
Exercise 1, Standby.replay: apply each whole record after replayLsn, up to upTo and never past flushLsn. stream calls it, so most other tests need it.

Exercise 2, Cluster.isAcknowledged: when has the primary answered a COMMIT? Off, local or no synchronous standby: at once. Otherwise compare the named standbys' write, flush or replay position with the record's end.

Exercise 3, Primary.checkpoint: mark slots that fell more than maxSlotWalKeepSize behind as lost, then remove the WAL every remaining slot already has. The tests stop a standby, write 500 commits, and check what the checkpoint keeps.

In Failover.kt, exercise 4 promotes the right standby and lists the acknowledged commits it never had, and exercise 5 replays a base backup and an archive up to a target time. Run the tests until all 27 pass.
hints: replay: val limit = minOf(upTo, flushLsn), then loop over wal: continue while record.end <= replayLsn, break at the first record.end > limit, otherwise applyRecord(record, data) and replayLsn = record.end.

checkpoint: the oldest restartLsn among slots that are not lost (or currentLsn if there are none) is where the WAL must start; every record with end <= that position can go. Mark lost slots first, so they don't hold anything.

failover: filter to running standbys within the lag limit, take maxByOrNull { it.flushLsn } (it keeps the first of equals), call its replay(), and the lost commits are acknowledged.filter { it.end > chosen.flushLsn }.

recover: track position, starting at the backup's LSN. Skip records that end at or before it; a record whose start != position is a hole. Stop at the first record past the target (with inclusive, committedAt > targetTime) and return; running out of records is an error too.

drill.title: A standby from nothing, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write what the primary needs for a new standby standby2 on 10.20.1.7 (the role, the slot, the pg_hba.conf line), the one command on the standby's host that clones the primary and makes it a standby, and the query on the primary that shows how many bytes the standby's replay is behind.

answer.html: -- on the primary CREATE ROLE replicator WITH REPLICATION LOGIN PASSWORD 'long-random-secret'; SELECT pg_create_physical_replication_slot('standby2', true); -- keeps WAL from now on -- pg_hba.conf, then SELECT pg_reload_conf(); -- hostssl replication replicator 10.20.1.7/32 scram-sha-256 -- on the standby's host, with an empty data directory: -- pg_basebackup -h primary -U replicator -D "$PGDATA" -X stream -S standby2 -R -c fast -- (-R writes standby.signal and primary_conninfo), then start PostgreSQL -- lag, on the primary SELECT application_name, state, sync_state, pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn) AS replay_behind_bytes, replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication;

recap: A standby is a copy of the data directory that never finishes crash recovery: it streams the primary's WAL and replays it onto the same pages. pg_basebackup -R -S builds one: the copy, standby.signal, primary_conninfo, and a slot.

A replication slot makes the primary keep WAL until its standby has it. A slot whose standby is gone keeps WAL until the disk fills; drop it, alert on inactive slots, and set max_slot_wal_keep_size or PostgreSQL 18's idle_replication_slot_timeout.
pg_stat_replication shows each standby's write, flush and replay positions and lags. Asynchronous replication, the default, acknowledges a commit before any standby has it, so a failover can lose it.

With synchronous_standby_names set, synchronous_commit chooses what COMMIT waits for: remote_write, on (flushed) or remote_apply (visible on the standby). A synchronous standby that is down makes commits wait; use two standbys with ANY 1.
Standby queries conflict with replay; after max_standby_streaming_delay they are cancelled. hot_standby_feedback trades the cancels for bloat on the primary.

Failover is pg_promote() plus fencing the old primary, or Patroni with a leader key in etcd. Backups are pg_dump, or a base backup plus archived WAL, which allows point-in-time recovery to just before a mistake. Test the restore.

explain.prompt: A product manager hears "we have a replica" and concludes the payments database can't lose a payment or go down for long. Explain what the replica does and doesn't protect against, and what it would take to get closer to that promise.
explain.answer: The replica is a second server that copies every change the primary makes, by streaming its write-ahead log and replaying it. If the primary's machine dies, we can promote the replica and be writing again in seconds to a minute, which protects against downtime. It doesn't promise no loss: by default the primary tells a client its payment committed before the replica has it, so the last fraction of a second of payments can be lost in a failover. Making the replica synchronous closes that gap, at a few milliseconds per commit, and then a dead replica would stop all writes, so we'd need two replicas and commit when either confirms. Someone or something also has to decide to fail over and make sure the old primary never comes back as a second primary; that's what Patroni or a managed service does. And the replica copies mistakes instantly: a bad DELETE is gone on both in milliseconds. For that we need backups, a base backup plus the archived WAL, so we can rebuild the database as it was a second before the mistake, and we need to test that restore regularly and know how long it takes.

deeper.html:
A delayed standby guards against mistakes. With recovery_min_apply_delay = '1h', a standby receives WAL at once but replays each commit only an hour after it happened. When someone runs a bad DELETE, you have an hour to pause its replay (pg_wal_replay_pause()) and copy the rows out, which is much faster than a point-in-time restore of a large database. It is never the standby you fail over to.

What did an asynchronous failover lose? The old primary's WAL after the point where the timelines split is still on its disk until you rewind it. Find the split point in the new primary's timeline history file (00000002.history in pg_wal), then run pg_waldump over the old primary's WAL from there: it prints each record, with the transaction ids and the relations they touched, so you can see which commits never reached the standby and replay them by hand if they matter.

Cascading replication lets a standby feed other standbys, so a remote data center can have three standbys and one cross-region stream. Cascaded standbys are always asynchronous.

Quorum commit generalizes ANY 1: synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 2 (s1, s2, s3)' waits for any two of three standbys, and survives losing one without stopping commits. It looks like Raft's majority rule (the Consistency and consensus track), with one difference: PostgreSQL itself does not elect a new primary from that majority, so the guarantee holds only if the failover tool promotes one of the standbys that confirmed.

Logical replication slots used to stay behind on the old primary at a failover, so subscribers broke. PostgreSQL 17 can synchronize them to a physical standby (sync_replication_slots = on on the standby, synchronized_standby_slots on the primary), so a subscription carries on from the new primary.

archive_command runs a shell command per segment. Since PostgreSQL 15, archive_library loads a module instead, which tools such as pgBackRest use for speed. Whichever you use, a failing archive keeps WAL on the primary just as a forgotten slot does: alert on pg_stat_archiver.failed_count.
